newsitem.title: USA: US oil markets awash with crude amid refinery work.
newsitem.headline: US oil markets awash with crude amid refinery work.

text.p: Oil markets are awash with crude amid abundant global supplies as refiner demand continues to suffer as the focus of U.S. refinery maintenance shifts to the midcontinent from the U.S. Gulf Coast.

"The Gulf Coast is now coming out of turnarounds, but the midcontinent still seems to be in full swing," said Tom Knight, a products trader with Fina Inc. "Everyone is expecting March to be full of turnarounds," Knight said.
Knight and others said the ongoing outages of various units was clearly having a bearish effect on crude prices.

Traders are saying large plants in Illinois operated by Mobil Corp at Joliet, Marathon Oil Co at Robinson, Shell Oil Co at Wood River and Clark Refining HSM.TO at Blue Island will all be conducting some sort of maintenance and or repairs during the month.
Also, Amoco Inc is said to be planning work at its large refining facility in Whiting, Indiana during April.

To make matters worse, many European refiners have cut utilization rates to offset weak prices they are fetching for their refined products. Also, refinery maintenance in Asia is sure to keep downward pressure on world crude prices as well.
"Refiner demand has temporarily been cut back while production has been going up like gangbusters," said Nizam Sharief, analyst with Hornsby & Co in Houston.
Traders said soft crude prices are setting the tone in U.S. energy markets since the seasonal increase in gasoline demand is not yet in full swing.
Sharief and others said crude supplies are growing increasingly abundant from Iraq, Latin American suppliers like Venezuela, Mexico and Colombia, and lately even West Africa.
Crude traders said wilting sweet and sour crude deltas were more the result of a supply glut than bad refiner demand.
"This is a situation of oversupply. Refiners can really go into the market and pick what they want," a crude trader said.
The bearish effects of mounting output are exacerbated by cuts in refinery utilization rates in Northwest Europe, which is sending even more crude supplies to the U.S. Gulf.
Two weeks ago week, West African barrels were the force behind a weakening differential for Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James, but last week traders have looked to the North Sea.
"There is Brent coming over here with Glencore. They seem to be dumping it on the market," said a trader with a major.
By Monday morning, the Louisiana Sweet grade had slid to 30 cents under the April WTI/Cushing marker, down sharply from the 20 cents premium it was fetching just over a week ago.
Analysts like Sharief said crude prices are likely to remain under downward pressure well into the northern hemisphere spring, since much of the Asian refinery work has not even started yet.
"The bulk of that Far East refinery maintenance will come in April and May," said Hornby's Sharief.
But some crude traders are saying they see evidence of Asian refiners already in turnarounds in the form of extra West African crudes on offer in U.S. Gulf Coast markets.

To be sure, about a million barrels a day of West African crudes mainly from Nigeria come into the Gulf Coast's "Refinery Row" every day, but the Asian refinery work and run cuts in Europe are pushing more of those crudes to the U.S.
Overall, they say that as prices continue to slide it is becoming increasingly clear that at the very least, oil stocks worldwide are higher than they were a year ago.

Indeed, the Paris-based International Energy Agency (IEA) said oil inventories at the end of February in the world's leading industrialized nations were higher than the year before for the first time in 18 months.
"A number of factors is leaving us with a bloated crude market," said Fina's Knight.
--Oliver Ludwig, New York Energy Desk ((+1 212 859 1620))
